title: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
objective: Stack and compare whole result sets: UNION ALL to append, UNION to append and de-duplicate, INTERSECT for 'in both', EXCEPT for 'in the first but not the second'.
context: Ledgers combine sales and refunds; reconciliation compares two lists of IDs; reports need a TOTAL row under the detail. Set operators work on entire result sets, matching columns by position.

exercises.title: Every customer ID we know about
exercises.question: Data governance wants the complete set of customer IDs referenced anywhere: the customer table or orders.
exercises.prompt: Return a single column customer_id with each distinct customer_id that appears in customers or in orders (each value once).
hints: You want distinct values from two sources, so UNION (not UNION ALL).
Both SELECTs return one column, customer_id.
SELECT customer_id FROM customers UNION SELECT customer_id FROM orders;
exercises.why: The result has 21 IDs. The extra one (99) is the orphan. Building a master key list with UNION is the first step of any reconciliation.

recall.q: What does UNION do that UNION ALL doesn't?
recall.a: It removes duplicate rows from the combined result (at the cost of a sort/hash).

exercises.title: Bought in both years
exercises.question: Retention wants the customers who made valid purchases in both 2024 and 2025.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id (from orders) for customers with at least one valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) dated in 2024 and at least one dated in 2025. Use INTERSECT.
hints: Two lists of customer_ids: 2024 buyers and 2025 buyers.
INTERSECT keeps values present in both lists (de-duplicated).
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE <valid> AND <2024> INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE <valid> AND <2025>;
exercises.why: Cross-period retention is a set intersection. INTERSECT states it directly, and it de-duplicates customers with several orders per year.

recall.q: Rewrite A INTERSECT B with EXISTS.
recall.a: SELECT DISTINCT ... FROM A WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.key = A.key).

exercises.title: Catalog items with no valid sale
exercises.question: Which catalog products have never been part of a valid order?
exercises.prompt: Return product_id for products in the catalog EXCEPT those that appear on a line of a valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded).
hints: First set: all product_ids. Second set: product_ids sold in valid orders.
EXCEPT returns rows of the first set that are not in the second.
SELECT product_id FROM products EXCEPT SELECT i.product_id FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ... WHERE <valid>;
exercises.why: Unlike NOT IN, EXCEPT is NULL-safe (NULLs compare equal in set operations). It's a clean way to diff two ID lists.

recall.q: What is Snowflake's synonym for EXCEPT?

exercises.snowflake: SELECT product_id FROM products MINUS SELECT ...;

exercises.title: Sales and refunds ledger by year
exercises.question: Accounting wants sales and refunds as separate ledger lines per calendar year.
exercises.prompt: Return activity_year, activity_type and amount. Stack (UNION ALL) two summaries: activity_type 'sale' with amount = gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), by year of order_date; and activity_type 'refund' with amount = -SUM(refund_amount) (negative), by year of return_date. Round amount to 2 decimals.
hints: Write the two grouped queries separately, each returning (year, label, amount).
Column names come from the first SELECT; the second just needs matching positions.

SELECT strftime('%Y', o.order_date) AS activity_year, 'sale' AS activity_type, ROUND(SUM(...),2) AS amount ... GROUP BY ... UNION ALL SELECT strftime('%Y', r.return_date), 'refund', ROUND(-SUM(r.refund_amount),2) FROM returns r GROUP BY ...;
exercises.why: Ledgers, event logs and activity feeds are built by stacking differently shaped sources into one shape. The literal label column is what keeps them distinguishable.

recall.q: Where do the output column names of a UNION ALL come from?

exercises.title: Net cash by year
exercises.question: Now finance wants a single net number per year: sales minus refunds (cash basis).
exercises.prompt: Return activity_year and net_amount, where net_amount = gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) (by order_date year) minus refund_amount (by return_date year), rounded to 2 decimals. Stack line-level sales and negative refunds with UNION ALL inside a derived table, then GROUP BY year.
hints: Make one tall table of (year, signed amount), then aggregate it.
Use UNION ALL, not UNION: two identical line amounts in the same year must both count.
SELECT activity_year, ROUND(SUM(amount),2) AS net_amount FROM (<sales lines> UNION ALL SELECT strftime('%Y', return_date), -refund_amount FROM returns) AS ledger GROUP BY activity_year;
exercises.why: With UNION instead of UNION ALL, identical (year, amount) rows would be collapsed and revenue silently under-stated. Line 150 duplicates line 96 (same order, same 96.90), and several unrelated lines share amounts too.

recall.q: Why is UNION (without ALL) dangerous when stacking amounts?
recall.a: It removes duplicate rows, so legitimately equal amounts get dropped.

exercises.title: Region report with a TOTAL row
exercises.question: The regional summary should end with a TOTAL line, like the spreadsheet it replaces.
exercises.prompt: Return region and customer_count: one row per region (NULL region shown as 'Unknown') with its number of customers, plus a final row with region = 'TOTAL' and the count of all customers. Sort region rows alphabetically, with TOTAL last.
hints: Detail rows (GROUP BY region) UNION ALL one total row.
To sort by a hidden key (TOTAL last), wrap the compound query in a derived table.
SELECT region, customer_count FROM (<detail> UNION ALL SELECT 'TOTAL', COUNT(*) FROM customers) t ORDER BY CASE WHEN region = 'TOTAL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, region;
exercises.why: Subtotal/total rows are a staple of finance reports. In Snowflake you would use GROUP BY ROLLUP; in portable SQL, UNION ALL plus a sort key does the job.

recall.q: Where may ORDER BY appear in a compound (UNION) query?
recall.a: Only once, at the end, applying to the whole combined result.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT COALESCE(region, 'Unknown'), COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY ROLLUP (COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')); (the rollup row has a NULL region; label it with GROUPING()).

exercises.title: Products popular in both North and South
exercises.question: Merchandising wants products that sell in both the North and South regions to plan a joint promotion.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name for products that appear in a valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) placed by a North-region customer AND in a valid order placed by a South-region customer. Use INTERSECT.
hints: Two queries with identical shape (product_id, product_name), differing only in region.
Each needs products → order_items → orders → customers joins.
<North query> INTERSECT <South query>; INTERSECT compares whole rows, so both columns must match.
exercises.why: INTERSECT compares entire rows. Selecting both id and name is fine because the name is a function of the id. Adding something that varies (like order_id) would break the logic.

recall.q: Does INTERSECT compare one column or the whole row?
recall.a: The whole row: every selected column must match.

worked_example.question: Reconcile customer IDs: which IDs appear in orders but not in customers, and vice versa?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT 'in orders, not customers' AS issue, customer_id
FROM (SELECT customer_id FROM orders EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM customers)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'in customers, not orders', customer_id
FROM (SELECT customer_id FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
ORDER BY issue, customer_id;
worked_example.explanation: Each EXCEPT returns distinct IDs from one side that are missing on the other. Wrapping them lets us add a label, and UNION ALL stacks the two findings. Order 31's customer 99 shows up on one side, and the three never-ordered customers on the other.

recipe:
**Recipe: line up the columns, then pick the operator**

1. Each SELECT must return the **same number of columns**, in the **same order**, with compatible types.
   Column **names come from the first SELECT**.
2. Choose:
   - `UNION ALL`: append everything (fast, keeps duplicates). **Default choice for stacking data.**
   - `UNION`: append, then remove duplicate rows (costs a sort; can silently drop legitimate duplicates).
   - `INTERSECT`: rows present in both. `EXCEPT`: rows in the first, not in the second (distinct).
3. Label the sources with a literal column so you can tell rows apart after stacking:
   ```sql
   SELECT 'sale'   AS activity_type, order_date  AS activity_date, ... FROM ...
   UNION ALL
   SELECT 'refund' AS activity_type, return_date AS activity_date, ... FROM returns;
   ```
4. `ORDER BY` goes once, at the very end, and refers to output columns. To aggregate or sort by a hidden key,
   wrap the whole compound query in a derived table: `SELECT ... FROM ( ... UNION ALL ... ) AS t GROUP BY ...`.
5. Set operators treat NULLs as equal to each other (unlike `=`), so a NULL row in both inputs INTERSECTs.
snowflake_notes:
- Snowflake supports `UNION [ALL]`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` and its synonym **`MINUS`**.
- Snowflake also has `UNION [ALL] BY NAME`, which matches columns by name instead of position.
  SQLite has no BY NAME, so always line columns up by position.
- For a TOTAL row, Snowflake can use `GROUP BY ROLLUP(region)` instead of a hand-made UNION ALL (SQLite has no ROLLUP).
common_mistakes: Using UNION when you meant UNION ALL, which silently drops duplicate rows (and is slower).
Mismatched column order: SQL matches by position, not name, so 'amount' can land under 'year'.
Putting ORDER BY inside each branch; it belongs once, at the end (or wrap in a derived table).
Forgetting a label column, so you can't tell which source a stacked row came from.
Adding a varying column to INTERSECT/EXCEPT selects, which changes what counts as 'the same row'.
recall: What must be true of the SELECTs combined by a set operator?
Same number of columns, in compatible types, in the same order.
How do set operators treat NULLs?
As equal to each other (unlike =), so NULL rows can match in INTERSECT/EXCEPT/UNION de-duplication.
